subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The belief that human beings are made 'in the image of God' is known by which term?
questions.explain: Imago Dei is Latin for 'image of God', drawn from Genesis 1:27, and underpins beliefs about human dignity and equality.

questions.q: In which year was the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted?
questions.explain: The UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948, setting out fundamental rights for all people.

questions.q: What does the belief in the 'sanctity of life' mean?
options: Only religious leaders' lives are sacred
Life must always be prolonged by machines
questions.explain: Sanctity of life is the belief that life is holy, precious and given by God, so it should be respected and protected.

questions.q: Which term best describes the suppression or banning of books, ideas or speech?
questions.explain: Censorship is the restriction of expression, which raises issues about freedom of religious and personal expression.

questions.q: The teaching 'there is neither Jew nor Greek... you are all one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28) mainly supports which idea?
questions.explain: This teaching stresses that all people are equal before God regardless of race, status or gender.

questions.q: A country bans citizens from openly practising or sharing their faith. Which human rights issue does this most directly raise?
questions.explain: Preventing people from practising or sharing their beliefs directly restricts freedom of religious expression.

questions.q: What does the term 'prejudice' mean?
options: Prejudging someone without proper knowledge of them
questions.explain: Prejudice is an unfair opinion formed about someone before knowing the relevant facts about them.

questions.q: How does 'discrimination' differ from prejudice?
options: It is acting on prejudiced attitudes
It is only a thought or feeling
It always means treating people fairly
It refers to giving to charity
questions.explain: Discrimination is putting prejudice into action, for example by treating someone unfairly in employment or services.

questions.q: Which leader promoted non-violent protest against racism during the American civil rights movement?
questions.explain: Martin Luther King Jr led non-violent campaigns against racial segregation and discrimination in the USA.

questions.q: Archbishop Desmond Tutu is best known for opposing which system of racial segregation?
questions.explain: Desmond Tutu was a Christian leader who campaigned against apartheid, the system of racial segregation in South Africa.

questions.q: What does the Parable of the Good Samaritan teach Christians about how to treat others?
options: Help anyone in need, regardless of their background
Only help members of their own religion
Give exactly one tenth of their income
questions.explain: The parable teaches that a 'neighbour' is anyone in need, challenging prejudice and encouraging compassion for all.

questions.q: In Islam, the worldwide community of Muslims, all equal before Allah, is called the:
questions.explain: The Ummah is the global community of Muslims, expressing the belief that all believers are equal regardless of race or wealth.

questions.q: What is meant by 'positive discrimination'?
options: Favouring a disadvantaged group to promote equality
Treating everyone in exactly the same way
Banning people from wearing religious dress
Refusing to employ people because of their age
questions.explain: Positive discrimination gives an advantage to a group that has been unfairly treated, aiming to create fairer outcomes.

questions.q: An employer refuses to promote a well-qualified worker only because she is a woman. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Discriminating against someone because of their gender is sexism, a form of unfair treatment condemned by most religions.

questions.q: In Islam, the compulsory annual giving of 2.5% of surplus wealth to help the poor is called:
questions.explain: Zakah is one of the Five Pillars of Islam, requiring Muslims to give 2.5% of their surplus wealth to those in need.

questions.q: Which Islamic term refers to charging interest on loans, which is forbidden?
questions.explain: Riba is the charging of interest, which is forbidden in Islam because it is seen as exploiting the poor.

questions.q: In Islam, what does 'Sadaqah' refer to?
questions.explain: Sadaqah is voluntary charity given out of generosity, in addition to the compulsory Zakah.

questions.q: A wealthy believer chooses to give away much of their income to help those in poverty. Which teaching best supports this decision?
options: 'The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil'
'An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth'
questions.explain: This teaching (1 Timothy 6:10) warns against greed and encourages using wealth responsibly to help others.

questions.q: The Christian practice of 'tithing' traditionally means giving what proportion of one's income?
options: Two and a half per cent (2.5%)
questions.explain: Tithing is the giving of one tenth of one's income, often to the Church or to help those in need.

questions.q: A Christian wants to fight global poverty by supporting a faith-based aid agency. Which organisation could they choose?
questions.explain: CAFOD is a Catholic overseas aid agency that works to relieve poverty and injustice around the world.

specSource: Eduqas GCSE Religious Studies specification; Component 3: Issues of Human Rights
